sermon:
## Paneled Houses and a House in Ruins
*The lie that says the time has not come yet*

**Text:** Haggai 1:1-11 · **Supporting:** Matthew 6:33; Deuteronomy 28:38-40; Luke 12:18-20; 1 Corinthians 3:16-17

Sixteen years. That is how long the foundation sat. The exiles had come home from Babylon, laid the first stones of the house of God, and then stopped. Not for a season. For sixteen years. And in all that time not one of them said out loud, we have decided not to build God's house. They said something more comfortable. They said the time had not come.

**The excuse that sounded like wisdom**
Hear how reasonable it is. "Thus says the Lord of hosts: These people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the Lord." (Haggai 1:2) Not, we refuse. Not, we have other gods. The time has not yet come. The economy is hard. The opposition is real, and it was — Ezra tells us the surrounding peoples had written to the empire and shut the work down for years. There were genuine obstacles. There always are. The excuse was not a fabrication. It was a fact bent into a permission slip.

We do the same thing, and we do it well. We do not say we have stopped following God. We say it is not the season. We will give when the raise comes. We will deal with the marriage when the kids are older. We will pray when life slows down. We have learned to dress neglect in the language of timing, and timing is a respectable word. It does not feel like rebellion. It feels like prudence. That is exactly why it holds for sixteen years.

And notice the date stamped on this word. It came in the second year of Darius, the king of Persia — a foreign emperor, a pagan court, the calendar of the people who had once carried them into exile. The remnant had come home, but they were still a small and frightened community ruled from a distant throne, surrounded by neighbors who wanted the work stopped. Their fear was not imaginary. The opposition was not invented. And God's word does not deny any of it. It simply refuses to let real fear become a permanent excuse. The obstacles were real. They were also not the reason. The reason was that the people had quietly decided their own comfort came first, and the obstacles were a cover story the heart was grateful to have.

**Consider your ways**
Then the word comes through the prophet, and it cuts past the excuse to the evidence. "Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?" (Haggai 1:4) Paneled. The word matters. Cedar paneling was finish work, the detail you add after the structure stands and the roof holds — the touch of a man who has time and money and craftsmanship to spare. They had the resources. They had the skill. They had the years. What they did not have was the will, and the proof was hanging on their own walls.

"Now, therefore, thus says the Lord of hosts: Consider your ways." (Haggai 1:5) Set your heart on your roads, the Hebrew says. Look at where your feet actually go, not where your mouth says they go. And then the Lord holds up the ledger. "You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough; you drink, but you never have your fill. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm. And he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes." (Haggai 1:6) Moses had promised this exact frustration to a covenant people who turned away — you will sow and the locust will eat it, you will plant and not gather (Deuteronomy 28:38-40). They were living inside their own Scriptures and could not see it.

Here is the line they missed, the one we miss. They thought they were managing a downturn. They blamed the rain, the soil, the markets, the neighbors. The Lord names it plainly: "Therefore the heavens above you have withheld the dew, and the earth has withheld its produce. And I have called for a drought on the land and the hills, on the grain, the new wine, the oil, on what the ground brings forth, on man and beast, and on all their labors." (Haggai 1:10-11) The empty harvest was not the economy. It was God. The holes in their pockets were not bad luck. They were a summons. He had been speaking to them through their own scarcity for years, and they read it as misfortune instead of mercy.

See the terrible patience in that. He did not strike them down for sixteen years of neglect. He let the fields come up thin and the wine run short and the wages disappear, and he did it on purpose, and he did it as a father, not a judge — disciplining a son he refused to lose. The discomfort they kept trying to fix with harder work was the very voice they kept refusing to hear. We do the same. We treat the restlessness, the dryness, the strange emptiness on the other side of the thing we were sure would satisfy, as a problem to be solved with more of the same. We rarely consider that the emptiness is a mercy, and that God may be making sure the bag has holes so that we will finally ask what we are filling it for.

**The house we leave in ruins**
Do not rush to feel superior to them. We are them. We have built our paneled houses and called the building wisdom. We pour ourselves into the career, the renovation, the portfolio, the body, the children's résumés — good things, every one, the way the temple's neighbors were good things — and we tell ourselves the house of God can wait for a more convenient year. I have done this from inside ministry. I have given God the leftover hour, the leftover dollar, the leftover attention, and called it a busy season, and then wondered why the harvest felt thin. The thinness was not the problem. It was the message.

And now lift it where Haggai's hammer was always swinging. "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16-17) The house in ruins is no longer made of cedar and stone. After the cross and Pentecost, the dwelling place of God is his people. When we finish our own houses and leave his in rubble, the rubble is us — the prayer life we never built, the holiness we keep deferring, the soul we panel on the outside and leave hollow within. "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." (Matthew 6:33) The man in Jesus' parable built bigger barns and heard, this night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:18-20). The barns were finished. The man was rubble.

The Lord of hosts is not asking for the time you have left over. He is asking why the house that bears his name is the one thing in your life you have not gotten around to. Consider your ways. Look at the roads your feet actually take. The drought was never the economy.

Your comfort indicts your priorities.

## They Obeyed, and I Am With You
*The four words God speaks into a first act of obedience*

**Text:** Haggai 1:12-15 · **Supporting:** Matthew 28:20; Exodus 33:14-16; Philippians 2:12-13; Isaiah 41:10

The word landed, and something almost never recorded in the prophets happened. They listened. Through Amos, through Jeremiah, through Isaiah, the pattern is the prophet speaks and the people harden. Here the prophet speaks and the people turn. Twenty-three days. From the first of the month to the twenty-fourth, the time it took for the message to reach the heart and the heart to reach the hands.

**The whole remnant, together**
Watch who obeyed. "Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the Lord their God." (Haggai 1:12) The governor, the man with the political authority. The high priest, the man with the spiritual authority. And all the remnant. Not a faction. Not the eager few who always show up. The whole body moved at once — leadership and people, throne and altar and street, the entire community turning on the same word in the same week.

That detail preaches before the sermon does. Obedience that stays at the top is policy. Obedience that stays at the bottom is grumbling. This was the rare thing — the leaders led and the people followed and no one was dragging anyone. They had spent sixteen years agreeing not to see the house in ruins. They spent twenty-three days agreeing to build it. And notice the verse adds, "and the people feared the Lord." The obedience was not management buy-in. It was the fear of God, which is the beginning of every real turning.

And weigh the word "obeyed" itself, because the text repeats it. They obeyed the voice of the Lord — and they obeyed the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him. The voice of God came to them through the voice of a man, an ordinary preacher, and they did not wait for a sign in the sky or a second confirmation or a more impressive messenger. The word was enough. That is the whole difference between a people who turn and a people who harden. The hardened always need more — more proof, more comfort, a better-timed season, a less inconvenient command. The remnant heard the word and moved. It had taken sixteen years of silence to bring them to this, but when the word finally landed on soft ground, it did not bounce. It took root in a week.

**The only words that matter**
Now comes the sentence the whole book is built around, and it is almost too short to notice. "Then Haggai, the messenger of the Lord, spoke to the people with the Lord's message, 'I am with you, declares the Lord.'" (Haggai 1:13) That is it. They obeyed, and into the obedience God spoke four words. Not, well done. Not, here is your reward. I am with you.

Those four words are the load-bearing wall of the whole Bible. They are what Moses begged for when the people had sinned and God threatened to send them up to the land without his presence. "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us?" (Exodus 33:14-16) Moses understood what we keep forgetting — the land was nothing without the presence. A finished temple full of God's absence is a tomb. A construction site full of God's presence is heaven on earth. The people had been chasing harvests. God offered them himself.

And hear where these words land. Not before the obedience, as a bribe. Not as the condition they had to meet first. The presence met them inside the first act of building. They picked up the tools, and the voice said, I am with you, declares the Lord. The God who seemed distant for sixteen silent years was speaking the moment they moved. He was never far. He was waiting on the other side of the obedience they kept deferring.

**Where his presence meets you**
This is where we get the order wrong, and getting it wrong keeps us paralyzed. We say, when I feel God with me, then I will obey. Haggai says, obey, and there he is. "And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel... and the spirit of Joshua... and the spirit of all the remnant of the people, and they came and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God." (Haggai 1:14) Look closely at that. The Lord stirred up their spirits — and they worked. Both are true in the same sentence. Paul says the same thing without a seam: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure." (Philippians 2:12-13) Their hands moved because his Spirit moved them, and his Spirit moved them as their hands moved. You do not have to untangle it. You only have to start.

I have stood with people waiting at the edge of an obedience they already knew was right — the hard conversation, the giving they had withheld, the sin they kept negotiating with — waiting to feel ready, waiting for some warmth to descend that would make it easy. It does not come first. It comes in the doing. The presence is not the prize at the end of the road. It is the companion you discover the moment you take the first step you have been refusing.

And this is the word the risen Christ leaves his church with, the same four, expanded by a cross. "And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." (Matthew 28:20) He says it not in a finished temple but at the start of an impossible assignment — go and make disciples — the same place Haggai's word landed: into the obedience, not after it. "Fear not, for I am with you." (Isaiah 41:10) The whole gospel is God closing the distance our sin opened, and the name of the child who does it is Immanuel, God with us. That is not a reward for the obedient. It is the reason the disobedient can ever begin.

Stop waiting to feel him before you obey him. Pick up the tool.

Obedience is where his presence meets you.

## The Latter Glory and the Signet Ring
*A promise spoken to a temple that looked like nothing*

**Text:** Haggai 2:1-23 · **Supporting:** Ezra 3:12-13; John 1:14; Hebrews 12:26-28; Jeremiah 22:24-30

The building had started, and then the discouragement came, and it came the way it always comes — through comparison. Less than a month into the work, the festival of Booths arrived, the feast that remembered the wilderness, and the old men in the crowd remembered something else. They remembered Solomon's temple. They had seen the first house in its glory, the gold and the cedar and the cherubim, before Babylon burned it. Now they looked at this foundation, this modest beginning, and they wept. Ezra records it: the sound of weeping could not be told apart from the sound of joy (Ezra 3:12-13). The young rejoiced at a temple. The old grieved at a shadow.

**Is it not as nothing in your eyes?**
God does not pretend the comparison is unfair. He names it before they can. "Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?" (Haggai 2:3) He says the discouraging thing out loud. It looks like nothing. Beside what was, it is nothing. He does not flatter the work. He does not tell them their little temple is secretly impressive. He agrees with their eyes and then refuses to let their eyes have the last word.

Three times he says it — to Zerubbabel, to Joshua, to all the people of the land — "Be strong... Work, for I am with you, declares the Lord of hosts, according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not." (Haggai 2:4-5) The strength does not come from a better-looking temple. It comes from a presence the temple cannot contain. Build, not because the building is glorious, but because I am here.

**The latter glory**
Then the promise breaks open, and it is far larger than the stones in front of them. "For thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts." (Haggai 2:6-7) The silver is mine, the gold is mine, he says — they were counting their poverty and God was counting his ownership of everything. And then the verdict that turned every weeping old man's grief inside out: "The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts. And in this place I will give peace." (Haggai 2:9)

Greater than Solomon's. They could not see it. The glory of this house would not be measured in gold leaf and cedar. It would be measured by who walked through its courts. The desire of all nations would come, and the glory that would fill the second temple was a glory no architect could draw. Five centuries later a carpenter from Nazareth stood in those same courts and "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father." (John 1:14) Dwelt — pitched his tent, tabernacled. The glory that filled the first temple as a cloud now walked the second on two feet. The old men wept because the building was small. They did not know the God of the building would one day be small enough to be held.

And the shaking was not finished. The writer of Hebrews takes up Haggai's exact words and stretches them to the end of all things: "Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens... that the things that cannot be shaken may remain." (Hebrews 12:26-28) The temple of Haggai's day fell again, to Rome in the year 70. The glory greater than Solomon's was never the masonry. It was the Lord of the house, and his kingdom cannot be shaken.

**The signet ring**
The book ends with one man and one promise, and it reaches back to undo a curse. The word comes to Zerubbabel, and to feel its weight you have to know his grandfather. Jehoiachin — Coniah — sat on David's throne and lost it, and over him God had pronounced a terrible word through Jeremiah: "Though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off." (Jeremiah 22:24-30) Record this man as childless, the prophet said. Write him down as a man whose offspring will not sit on David's throne. The royal line looked severed at the root.

Now hear God speak to that man's grandson, a governor with no crown, building a temple that looked like nothing. "On that day, declares the Lord of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the Lord, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the Lord of hosts." (Haggai 2:23) The signet that was torn off is put back on. The curse is reversed. The line that looked dead is kept alive, and Zerubbabel's name stands in both genealogies of Jesus, Matthew's and Luke's, a link in the chain that runs from David to the manger. God preserved the messianic promise through a discouraged man building a disappointing temple in an unimportant year.

So do not despise the day of small things, and do not measure God's work by what your eyes can total up. I have stood in rooms where faithful people grieved that their labor looked like nothing beside what they remembered, beside what others built, beside what they had hoped — the small church, the slow obedience, the unseen years. I have grieved it myself, counting the gold leaf and missing the presence. The old men wept over a foundation while the God of glory was promising to walk it. The glory you cannot see has always been the only glory that lasts, and it is coming, and it has a name.

The glory you cannot see is coming.
